summary: For ages 5–7, this is a naming-and-noticing topic: children identify the Sun, Moon and stars as objects in the sky and describe their most obvious observable differences. The Sun is a bright source of light and heat we see by day; stars are tiny points of light we see at night; the Moon changes and can appear in the daytime sky as well as at night. The priority is rich first-hand observation and accurate everyday language, not explanation of causes. Two early points matter: never look directly at the Sun, and at this stage the Sun 'gives us light and heat' while the Moon is simply an object we can see (the reflected-light explanation comes later). Activities centre on a day/night sky to sort and name objects, a home sky diary grounded in children's own observation, and consolidation sorting and short checks.
misconceptions: Stars only exist at night / disappear or 'go out' in the daytime (they are still there but the Sun's brightness hides them)
The Moon only comes out at night (it is often visible in the daytime sky)
The Sun is not a star / is completely different in kind from stars (it is a star — foreshadow only; formalised in the next topic)
The Sun moves round the Earth or 'goes away' at night to another place (the appearance of movement; cause not needed yet but avoid entrenching a travelling-Sun story)
The Sun, Moon and stars are all roughly the same distance / size as they appear (huge differences in size and distance hidden by how they look)

activities.title: Day sky / night sky: name what you see
steps: Look at a day-sky scene and a night-sky scene side by side (or a single scene you can switch between day and night).
Point to and name the Sun in the day sky; say that the Sun gives us light and heat.
Say the sun-safety rule aloud: we never look straight at the Sun because it is so bright it can hurt our eyes.
Point to and name the stars as tiny points of light seen at night.
Point to and name the Moon; looking at the sky away from the Sun, find that a pale Moon can also appear in the day sky.

Tap or lift a flap on each object to check its name and a short fact: Sun — 'gives us light and heat; never look straight at it'; star — 'other suns, very far away'; Moon — reveal a real photo of the Moon in a blue daytime sky.
activities.insight: The Sun, Moon and stars are distinct objects in the sky with different observable properties, and the Moon is not only a night-time object — it can be seen in the daytime too.

activities.title: Our sky diary: watch and record
steps: Over several days or weeks, record when you see the Sun, Moon and stars — at home and at school. Never look straight at the Sun; just notice that it is up and record the time of day.
Draw or note what you saw and when (day or night).
Especially try to catch and record the Moon when it is visible in the daytime — look at the part of the sky away from the Sun to find it safely.
Share your diary and talk about any day when you saw both the Sun and the Moon at the same time.
activities.insight: Through your own repeated observation, the Moon is a sky object seen at different times (day or night), not a night-only lamp, while the Sun is seen by day and stars are seen at night.

activities.title: Sort and compare: day, night, or both
steps: Watch a sky change from day to night (for example, drag a sun-clock from day to night and see the Sun set and stars emerge).
Sort cards for the Sun, Moon and star into 'day sky', 'night sky' and 'both' bins.
Build a simple compare-and-contrast chart: for the Sun, Moon and star, answer 'day or night?', 'gives us daylight and warmth we can feel?', and 'big and bright or tiny to us?'.
Explain your sorting out loud — especially why the Moon can go in 'both'.
activities.insight: The three objects can be told apart and grouped by their observable properties, and the Moon belongs in 'both' because it can appear by day and by night.

activities.title: Quick check: which one is it?
steps: Answer a short picture check: 'Which one gives us light and heat?'
Sort objects into day / night / both.
Match each object to its name using photos.
activities.insight: You can reliably name the Sun, Moon and stars and recall their key observable differences.

checkQuestion: It's the middle of the afternoon and the Sun is out. Could you ever look up and see the Moon in the sky right now? Tell me yes or no — and HOW you know.
checkAnswer: Yes. The Moon can often be seen in the daytime sky as a pale shape, because on many days it is up in the sky at the same time as the Sun — it is not only a night-time object. (The stars are still up there in the daytime too, but we can't see them because the Sun's light is far too bright.)
